column9: Corrected 2026-09-23. Two numerical forms exist. SSLG4 distributes a 77-point table for NaI(Tl), attributed to a manufacturer (Luxium Solutions), without conditions or uncertainty. And Fig. 2 of Mao et al. (2008) -- the figure the attenuation curve is digitised from -- draws the photoluminescence band of the same sample, measured with a fluorescence spectrophotometer at a geometry chosen so that internal absorption does not shape it; digitised on the same axis it peaks at 409 nm with a 90 nm FWHM. It is excited by ultraviolet light, not ionising radiation. Miller et al. plot a band (Fig. 8b) whose data sit behind an IEEE DataPort subscription; the LBNL library lists the 415 nm peak only. No measured scintillation spectrum with its conditions was located, so the band shape remains an assumption; the two numerical bands are run as variants.

column9: The parameter set is fitted to a 25.4 mm cube. The canonical 7.0 % FWHM benchmark refers to a 76.2 x 76.2 mm cylinder. Light collection differs between the two, so the parameters and the benchmark are not describing the same detector -- which is precisely the correction Paper 0 exists to make.

column3: any simulation that digitises a published emission curve
column5: (convention, not a measurement): Geant4 11.4.2 G4Scintillation::BuildInverseCdfTable integrates the table over photon ENERGY
column9: The values in a SCINTILLATIONCOMPONENT table are a probability density in energy, but published emission curves are plotted against wavelength. Tabulating such a curve directly makes Geant4 sample p(lambda) proportional to w(lambda)/lambda^2 -- blue-shifted by 2 sigma^2 / lambda_0. For a 415 nm band of 65 nm FWHM: written 415.00 nm, analytic expectation 411.24 nm, measured in simulation 411.25 nm. The shift is toward the absorption edge, so it increases self-absorption.

column3: any simulation that counts optical photons
column5: (not applicable): G4OpticalPhysics enables Cerenkov alongside Scintillation
column9: Optical photons are not all scintillation photons. In NaI (n ~ 1.85) the Cerenkov threshold for electrons is ~96 keV, which Compton electrons from 662 keV gammas pass. Measured here: 27.7 Cerenkov photons per full-energy event, 0.102 % of the scintillation photons; counted with them, the photon-budget gate shows a +0.090 % excess at 4.9 standard deviations (corrected 2026-09-23 from the figures of an earlier campaign). Negligible for NaI; not negligible for a dense high-index crystal or at higher energy.

column5: Mao Zhang & Zhu (2008), Perkin Elmer Lambda-950 double-beam transmittance, 1.5 X0 = 38.8 mm NaI(Tl) cylinder, sealed in quartz windows
column9: No longer a scanned slope: the curve is digitised and inverted, so the shape across the emission band is measured rather than assumed. Two independent checks pass -- the wavelength calibration reproduces the emission (410 nm) and excitation (346 nm) peaks printed inside the panel to within 2.5 nm, and the recovered 50 %% cut-off is 361.3 nm against the 365 nm the paper states in its text. Remaining limits: it is an EFFECTIVE attenuation (a single-beam transmittance does not separate absorption from scattering), and the inversion is ill-conditioned above ~450 nm where the measured transmittance approaches its Fresnel limit (+-15 %% at 450 nm, +-24 %% at 500 nm).
